value.overview: The Western Wood-Pewee is a small, migratory tyrant flycatcher of open forests and woodland edges. It breeds mainly across western North America and spends the nonbreeding season in tropical regions of the Americas. The species is usually inconspicuous when perched, but its repeated sallies from exposed branches and distinctive, rough descending call make it easier to detect. In Costa Rica it is an uncommon migrant and winter visitor, and identification should be confirmed carefully because it resembles the Eastern Wood-Pewee.
value.classification: The Western Wood-Pewee belongs to the order Passeriformes and the flycatcher family Tyrannidae. Its scientific name is Contopus sordidulus.
value.identification: Adults are plain grayish-brown above with whitish underparts, a smudgy gray breast band and sides, two pale wingbars, and little or no obvious eye-ring. The bill is mostly dark, often with a paler or yellowish base to the lower mandible. It has a fairly upright posture, long wings, and a straight-looking tail. It is extremely similar to the Eastern Wood-Pewee, so the rough, nasal, slightly descending call is often the most dependable field mark, especially in Costa Rica.
value.rangeHabitat: The species breeds from Alaska and western Canada through the western United States and parts of northern Mexico. It migrates south through Mexico and Central America to wintering areas in northern and western South America. In Costa Rica, it occurs mainly as an uncommon migrant or winter visitor rather than a regular breeder; records may be scattered because silent Contopus flycatchers are difficult to identify. It uses open woodland, forest edges, riparian trees, secondary woodland, plantations, and other places with prominent perches and open flight space.
value.migrationStatus: A long-distance Neotropical migrant. In Costa Rica it is generally a scarce passage migrant and uncommon winter visitor, with occurrence concentrated during migration and the northern winter; it is not considered a regular breeding species there.
value.breeding: Breeding occurs mainly in open coniferous, mixed, deciduous, and riparian woodland across western North America. The nest is a small, shallow cup built on a horizontal or slightly sloping tree branch, often several metres above the ground. It is made from grasses, plant fibers, lichens, bark strips, and spider web. The female usually lays a small clutch of pale eggs marked with darker spots. Costa Rica lies outside the species’ normal established breeding range.
value.dietFeeding: Western Wood-Pewees feed chiefly on flying insects, including beetles, moths, flies, wasps, bees, and other small arthropods. They usually wait on an exposed branch, scan the surrounding air, and launch on a short, rapid flight to seize prey before returning to the same or a nearby perch. They may also take insects from vegetation and occasionally eat small fruits, particularly when flying insects are less available.
value.behavior: This species is typically solitary or found singly, although migrants may occur in loose concentrations where food is abundant. It spends much of the day perched upright in the canopy or along woodland edges, repeatedly making short flycatching flights. Individuals often return to a favored perch and may flutter their wings on landing. The song is a characteristic rough, buzzy, descending call. It defends breeding territories and can become vocal around dawn, dusk, and during nest defense.

conservation.populationTrend: The overall population is considered to be declining, although trends vary among regions and monitoring programs. The decline has not placed the species in a globally threatened category.
conservation.threats: Loss and degradation of mature woodland and riparian habitat on breeding and wintering grounds are important concerns. Habitat conversion, forest fragmentation, reduced insect abundance, pesticide exposure, and changing climate conditions may also affect survival and breeding success. Because the species depends on flying insects, prolonged cold or drought during migration can reduce feeding opportunities.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore open woodland, riparian forest, and mature tropical forest throughout its range, including wintering habitat in Central America. Reduce unnecessary pesticide use and maintain native trees, dead branches, and insect-rich vegetation. Support bird monitoring and habitat conservation, and report well-documented Costa Rican sightings with photographs or recordings because the species is uncommon there and can be confused with the Eastern Wood-Pewee.
